p: Friday, February 4, 2061. 5:25 AM. Sam hadn't slept. Around three he'd stopped pretending and printed AR 2207 on the printer in Ada's room, the one with the cartoon tomato sticker she'd stuck on the lid when she was eleven. At a quarter to five he'd put his boots on and driven east on I-70 in the dark, with the printout face up on the passenger seat, as if it wanted to see where they were going.

The test stand was two miles past the high bay on a gravel road the county had stopped plowing in 2050. In the dark it was a tower of white lights standing in the middle of nothing, with the departure stage bolted into it, frost blankets over its lower half like somebody had tucked it in. The wind came across the prairie with nothing to stop it between here and Kansas and leaned on the truck hard enough that he felt it in the wheel. Wendell Price's pickup was already in the lot. It was always already in the lot.

Wendell was in the blockhouse with his boots up on a cable tray and the lid of a thermos balanced on his knee, watching four screens that showed the stage from four sides. He didn't turn around. You found Bea's folder.
Nobody drives out here at five in the morning to look at a building. He took his boots off the tray. She was going to ask me about it. December. She had it on a sticky note.
Sam thought of the note on the bezel of Bea's monitor, square capitals. ASK W ABOUT STAND. He'd read it every morning for four weeks and taken it for a reminder about a seal.

No. She ran out of December. He pointed at the third screen, at a gray cylinder about the size of a beer keg low on the stage, in a nest of lines, wrapped in its own blanket. That's her. Main oxidizer isolation valve. August of '59, she twitched on cycle three. Forty milliseconds. We cycled her twice more that afternoon and she was perfect both times.
Stand had noise that summer. Ground fault on the instrumentation bus, June till we found it in September. Three channels spiking. I wrote it up.

Wendell looked at him for the first time. I said the stand had noise. Nobody asked me if that valve did. They asked if the stand had noise that summer, and I said yes, because it did. He picked up the thermos lid, found it empty, and set it down again. Pull the file. Look at the pressure channel downstream of her. Then come back out here and ask me the right question.

By 8:30 the file was on the big screen in the program room, and Quinn had it plotted. She'd come in at seven without being asked, because she'd seen his truck in the lot at six, which he'd forgotten she would.

STAND 2 DATA MOIV-1 ACCEPTANCE MON AUG 18 2059 CYCLE 3 OF 5. T+0 MS: CLOSE COMMAND.. T+208 MS: LVDT POSITION AT CLOSED. LIMIT SWITCH CLOSED.. T+214 TO T+254 MS: LVDT REPORTS POPPET 0.4 MM OFF SEAT. LIMIT SWITCH CLOSED. (DISAGREEMENT 40 MS.). T+254 MS: LVDT AT CLOSED. AGREEMENT RESTORED.. CH 31, DOWNSTREAM PRESSURE (RACK B): RIPPLE, 3.1 PSI PEAK, T+216 TO T+251 MS.. NOTE: CH 31 ON RACK B. LVDT ON RACK A. BOTH RACKS ON INSTRUMENTATION GROUND BUS 2.

Quinn put her finger on the screen, on the little hump in channel 31. That's on a different rack. If it's noise, it's noise that happened on two racks at once and knew exactly when to start. She read the last line again. Same ground bus, though. She sat back. So it's the valve coming off its seat and letting a little oxygen past, or it's the ground fault, and this file can't tell you which. Two retests, same afternoon, same stand, same crew, same ground fault. She had both hands flat on the table.
At 8:55 Hana Iwasaki came in early for the nine o'clock with her laptop under her arm, saw the plot on the wall, and stopped a step inside the door.

That's closed, she said. She said it to the plot. She didn't look at Sam. She set her laptop down on the table, picked it back up, said she'd be at the stand, and left, and the door took its time closing behind her on the pneumatic arm.
She was in the room when it closed, Quinn said quietly. Everybody was.

Sam looked at the forty milliseconds for a long time after Quinn went to get coffee. He knew what this was. A form somebody had closed with a doubt still behind it. He knew how that felt from the inside, because once, in Arizona, in 2041, he'd been the one holding the pen, with an indication on a jet that came and went and an hour he didn't have. He didn't think about that, as a rule. The rule had held for nineteen years. It wasn't holding this morning.

At 9:14 Garrett's email came in. Sam. Readiness Board wants the integrated plan for its March 21 session. All of it. Let's talk Monday. G. Over the high bay doors the countdown clock said 744. Sam folded the printout of AR 2207 in half and put it in his desk drawer. Then he took it back out and laid it flat on top of the desk, where he'd have to look at it.
Ruth's Console Log, page two: the gate and the bars.

Ruth's console log. Petrel Flow. L Minus 385 Days. May 23 2034. oh six thirty, integrated timeline up on the wall, flow 3. eleven sheets, taped end to end. wendell says the tape will outlast the program. oh seven hundred, every subsystem drew its own bars. prop. gnc. hab. crew. range. nobody's bars touch anybody else's. that's a lie. went down the wall with the red marker. oh eight forty, 41 places where the bars touch. nobody owns any of them. I do now. oh nine fifteen, drew the window at the right edge. two lines. mori says it looks like a gate. oh nine sixteen, it is a gate. oh nine twenty, across the top: the gate is real. the bars in front of it are guesses. eleven hundred, administrator walked through. asked why the bars have fuzzy ends. told him because they do. fourteen hundred, scope review. what petrel won't carry. tate asked for her keyboard. 4 kg. denied. she said she'll hum. seventeen thirty, L minus 385. tape holding.

That's me in May of 2034, five weeks into the job. I was proud of the red marker. I'd never seen anyone go down a wall of other people's schedules circling the places where they touched, and I thought I'd invented something. I hadn't. I'd found out what an integrated plan is for.

The ECO's first Process task is develop an integrated project management plan and plan delivery. You met the front half of its enablers on page one: assess the project's needs and complexity, recommend an approach. The rest are about the plan itself. Create it. Estimate the effort and the resources. Assess the consolidated plans for dependencies, gaps, and continued business value. Maintain it. Collect and analyze data so the decisions it drives are informed ones.

The integrated plan is the document that says how the project will be done, watched, and closed. It pulls together the subsidiary plans for scope, schedule, cost, quality, resources, communications, risk, procurement, and stakeholder engagement, plus the baselines the work gets measured against. Most of those plans have owners other than you. The leads should write their own parts, because a plan is how people agree to work together, and nobody agrees to a plan somebody else wrote for them. You own the whole thing, and you own the places where the parts touch. Each of my eleven sheets was a good plan. The forty one red circles were where the program would actually come apart, because nobody had to answer for them.

The PMBOK Guide's eighth edition names a holistic view among its principles. That's this wall. In a hybrid project the agile team's release plan and cadence belong inside the integrated plan, with the dates where its work meets the hardware fixed and owned. A board covered in sticky notes is a perfectly good plan for software. It's one part of a plan for a ship.

And the gate. Write my 0920 line next to whatever you're planning. The window is a constraint, about as hard as constraints get. Every bar in front of it is an estimate somebody made on a particular Tuesday. A plan that treats its estimates as if they were the gate will break the first time one of them turns out to be a guess. Every one of them is.

How the exam asks it. If a question asks who owns the integrated plan, it's the project manager, built with the team. If it asks what to update after an approved change, think of the plan and its baselines, not just the schedule.

At 1400 that day we held the scope review, and Roz Tate asked to bring her keyboard. An electric piano, four kilos with the stand. She played it in the evenings in the crew quarters at the Cape, the same six songs, not well, and Lise said she'd fly the ship to Mars by hand if it meant never hearing the fourth one again. We said no. Mass. It's on page two in my handwriting, and I've read that line more times than anything else on the page.

The ECO's R2 is develop and manage project scope, and its enablers are short: define scope, obtain stakeholder agreement on project scope, break down scope. You define it in the project scope statement. It describes the product and the project's deliverables, the acceptance criteria for each, the assumptions you're making, the constraints you're under, and what's excluded.

Exclusions are the part people skip, and they're the part that matters most later. Every stakeholder carries a picture of what the project will deliver. Wherever that picture runs past what you're building, you have an argument coming. Writing the exclusion down with its reason, in words a family member could read, is how you have that argument early, while it's cheap. Leave it for launch day and it costs you everybody's trust at once.

Then get the agreement. Defining scope is the project's job. Agreeing to it belongs to the stakeholders it touches, and for the hard exclusions that means sitting down with the people they hurt before the document reaches them.

Two words the exam likes. Scope creep is uncontrolled growth in scope, usually one small, reasonable request at a time. Gold plating is the team adding things nobody asked for, because it could. Both skip the agreement step, and both cost mass, whatever your project's version of mass happens to be.

How the exam asks it. When stakeholders assume something is included that isn't, clarify the scope with them and document the exclusion. Quietly adding it is scope creep, and promising to study it to keep them happy sets up a bigger gap.

Now break it down. A work breakdown structure is a hierarchy that decomposes the total scope of the project, deliverable by deliverable, until you reach work packages: pieces small enough to estimate, schedule, cost, and hand to one owner. The WBS dictionary describes each element, what it is, what done looks like, who owns it, what it depends on. The approved scope statement, the WBS, and the WBS dictionary together are the scope baseline.

Two rules carry most of the weight. Decompose by deliverable. A WBS organized by department tells you who sits where and hides everything that falls between the desks. Then check the 100 percent rule: the children of any element add up to all of the parent's work and nothing outside it. Check that honestly and you find the work nobody owned. There's always some.

Then the backlog. A product backlog is an ordered list of everything the team might build for the product, ranked by value and refined continuously by the product owner. The items near the top are small, clear, and ready. The ones near the bottom are coarse, and they're supposed to be. It changes every sprint, and that's what it's for.

In a hybrid project you don't have to pick one. The WBS holds the whole scope, and one element of it, the software, gets delivered adaptively. That element's content is the backlog. Its releases are tied to integration dates in the schedule. Anything in the backlog that needs hardware names the WBS element it touches, so a new feature that needs a new sensor turns up as a hardware question while there's still time to buy the sensor. Planning near work in detail and far work in outline, and adding detail as you learn, is rolling wave planning, and it works on both sides of the seam.

How the exam asks it. Work discovered late, owned by nobody, usually points to the 100 percent rule. In hybrid scenarios, pick the answer that keeps one scope, with the adaptive part delivered from a backlog and joined to the plan at defined milestones.

R8, plan and manage schedule, has enablers worth reading slowly: prepare a schedule based on the selected development approach, coordinate with other projects and operations, estimate, use benchmarks and history, create the schedule, baseline it, run the schedule management plan, analyze variation. Notice the order. You baseline after the estimates have come from the people doing the work, and after you've checked the schedule against everything else that needs the same people and the same facilities. A stand that's down for a seal change is operations, and operations doesn't read your schedule.

A baseline is the approved version of the schedule, and later of the scope and the cost, that progress gets measured against. It's approved through governance, usually by the sponsor, and it changes only through change control. In a hybrid project you baseline hardware in detail and software at the release level, and leave the backlog free to move underneath. Baselining every user story turns ordinary backlog refinement into a weekly flood of variances that mean nothing.

Which brings me to change control, the ECO's B3: execute the change control process, communicate the status of proposed changes, implement approved changes, update the documentation. The process is plain. Someone asks for a change. It gets written down as a change request. The people who'd do the work analyze its impact on scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk, and people. A change control board, or whoever your governance names, decides at the right level. The plan and its baselines get updated. The person who asked hears where it stands, including when the answer is no.

Every change goes through that, whoever asks. A sponsor's request is a change request with an important name on it. On an agile team, reordering the backlog inside a release is the product owner's ordinary work and doesn't need a board. When a change crosses the baseline, or the seam between the software and the hardware, it goes through change control, however small and quick the team that would build it.

How the exam asks it. The first move with a change request is usually to analyze its impact. Implementing it before approval, or turning it down on your own, are the traps, even when the request comes from the sponsor.
A list of how people die.

My register in 2034 had six hundred lines and not one of them had a person in it. We wrote in codes. Prop margin. Thermal concern. We knew what the codes meant. Codes let you read six hundred lines a week without feeling any of them, and I think that was the point of them, and I think it was a mistake.

B5 is plan and manage risk: identify risks, analyze them, develop the risk management plan, maintain the register, execute the responses, monitor and control, and communicate the status of each risk's impact. A risk is an uncertain event or condition that would affect the project, for better or worse, if it happened. An issue is one that has happened. The register carries each risk's cause, event, and effect, its probability and impact, an owner, a planned response, and the trigger that tells you it's starting.

Here's what I want you to keep. Probability and impact are separate axes, and you assess them separately. Impact comes from the consequence: what happens, and to whom, if this goes wrong. Probability comes from the evidence. The quickest way to talk yourself out of a risk is to let one leak into the other, to call a failure less serious because it seems unlikely. On flight programs the impact scale often has its own name, criticality, set by the worst credible consequence of the failure mode. Criticality 1 means you could lose the crew or the vehicle. How often you think it'll happen doesn't come into it.

Write your risks so a tired person can read them. If this happens, then this, and this is who gets hurt. And when you don't know the likelihood, write unknown. A one means you know it's rare. The register is no place to guess politely.
How the exam asks it. If a scenario lowers a risk's impact because the event seems rare, it's mixing the axes. Impact follows the consequence. Probability follows the evidence.
Rules, and the ways around them.

B2 is plan and manage project compliance. Confirm the compliance requirements; the ECO's examples are security, health and safety, sustainability, and regulatory compliance. Classify them. Determine the potential threats to compliance. Use methods that support it. Analyze the consequences of noncompliance. Decide what to do. Measure how far the project actually complies.

A flight rule is a compliance requirement in the safety category, and on a program like Halcyon it binds. Code 2.3.1, a mandatory standard, says we inform ourselves of, and uphold, the policies, rules, regulations, and laws that govern our work. Upholding a rule includes upholding what it's for.

The threat to compliance you'll meet most often isn't somebody breaking a rule. It's somebody finding its edge. A rule applies above a threshold, so the item gets classified just under the threshold. A review kicks in above a dollar figure, so the order gets split in two. Each instance looks fine on its own. When the same move turns up more than once, near the same kind of deadline, you have a pattern, and the pattern is the finding. Measure it, report it to the governance that owns the rule, and propose a control that closes the edge.

There's a rule in the ARA's book with my initials on it. I'll tell you about it when we get there. For now I'll only say that the person who writes a rule knows exactly where its edges are, and lies awake about them.

How the exam asks it. For compliance problems, the best answer measures the extent of the problem and reports it through governance. Quietly fixing the records, or certifying that the letter of the rule was met, are the distractors.
Sooner or later you'll find something closed that shouldn't have been. A report, a decision, a test. Somebody you respect signed it, everyone around you is tired, and opening it will cost weeks.

The Code is plain about what you owe. 2.2.5: when we make or discover errors or omissions, ours or anyone else's, we take prompt corrective action, and we tell the appropriate authority as soon as we find them. 5.2.1: we earnestly seek to understand the truth. And 5.3.1, from page one, rules out withholding what would make your statements misleading. A closed report you don't believe in is a statement.

It's just as plain about how. 3.2.3: we actively listen to other people's points of view, seeking to understand them. 3.2.7: when we disagree with someone, we ideally go to them directly. So you go to the person who made the call first, privately, with the evidence, and you listen. Almost nobody closes a crit 1 report out of malice. They close it because they believed something, or feared something, usually both at once. 5.2.5 asks you to build an environment where people feel safe to tell the truth, and 2.3.5, a mandatory standard, says we don't retaliate against anyone for raising a good faith ethical concern. The person who signed the closure often has the most to tell you once it's open, if you haven't made an enemy of them on the way.

Then you use the process, formally, where people can see it. A quiet look in a drawer doesn't count. A fresh piece of paper stapled to the old one doesn't either. Ethical failures on projects are nearly always organizational: a tired room, a date, a dozen people who each did one small reasonable thing. The Code still asks each person in that room to speak. On this page, that's you.

How the exam asks it. When a scenario involves a colleague's questionable decision, the best first step is usually a private conversation to understand it, then the formal process. Public confrontation and silence are both distractors.

The last task on this page is P6, manage stakeholder expectations. Its enablers are about customers, internal and external: identify their expectations, align and maintain the outcomes to them, monitor their satisfaction, and respond as needed. On Halcyon the external customers are 212 people on Mars and the families who'd give a great deal to hear them breathe.

Managing expectations starts with finding out what they are. Then you tell people the truth about what the project will and won't do, and you work on the distance between the two. When you sit down with someone whose expectation you can't meet, the answer you came to give is rarely the most useful thing in the room. What they need instead usually is, and some of it you can do.

Our families in 2035 got a newsletter. It had a photo of the crew on the front and a paragraph from me, and I signed it every month. I kept copies. I don't think there's a sentence of mine in any of them that would survive one of those families reading it today.
That's page two. The gate is real. Everything in front of it is a guess. Plan like you know the difference.
How the exam asks it. When a stakeholder expects something out of scope, meet them, clarify honestly, and agree on what they can expect. Promising a study to keep them happy only widens the gap.

Monday, February 7. Garrett came down to the program room himself at 7:40, which he never did, with a coffee from the place in Bennett and a printout of the board clerk's email. The Independent Readiness Board would meet on March 21 and wanted, the clerk wrote, "the program's integrated project management plan." Someone had underlined integrated twice, and it hadn't been Garrett.

Quinn had pulled together everything that might count. The integrated master schedule, thirty one thousand lines. A risk management plan from 2059 describing a risk review board that had last met in the spring. A quality plan that lived at Aldergrove and referred to Tallgrass as "the customer." Rafa's release plan, which was a board in his team's tool covered in colored notes. The procurement terms, which were inside four contracts. The communication plan for the Breather work. Nothing joined any of them to any of the others. Nobody's name was on the whole thing, because there wasn't a whole thing.
It's eleven documents and a board, she said. I don't think it's a plan. I think it's a pile.
The board wants an integrated plan by March 21, and Garrett says send them the plan. What should Sam do?
A. Send the board the master schedule, the risk plan, and the other documents as they are.
B. Make Quinn the plan's owner and have her collect a section from each lead.
C. Have each lead write their own section and join them into one plan he owns himself.
D. Hire Garrett's consulting firm to write the integrated plan for the leads to review.

Sam puts every lead's name on a one page table, with the section each one owns and the date it's due. Then he and Quinn spend two evenings on the part nobody owns, the joints. Where the risk plan's reviews feed the schedule. Where Aldergrove's quality plan has to hand its test data to Wendell. Where Rafa's release plan lands on the hardware's red dates. They find thirty six places where two documents assume different things. Hana reads the list and says, Thirty six. I'd have bet forty. It's the first joke she's made anywhere near him in a week, and she still doesn't quite look at him while she makes it.

That's a go. The integrated plan joins the subsidiary plans and the baselines into one document that says how the project gets run, watched, and closed. The leads own their parts. You own the whole, and the seams most of all, because a gap between two good plans is still a gap. Then you keep it current.

Tuesday, February 8. Hana had missed Monday's leads meeting with a calendar note that said stand. She'd missed Tuesday's standup with a note that said stand. Wendell, asked, said she'd spent both days out there running leak checks that didn't need her.
Sam had the stand file on his laptop and the pressure trace printed and folded in his jacket. He had the feeling, which he didn't like, that the whole building knew what was in his jacket.

Rafa caught him in the hall by the vending machines. Whatever it is, she's been carrying it since before you got here, he said, which was more than Rafa usually said about anyone on the hardware side. Just so you know.
Sam has the old pressure trace folded in his jacket. What should he do first?
A. Ask Garrett what he remembers about the 2059 downgrade before raising it with Hana.
B. Pull the raw 2059 data from Wendell and Aldergrove first, then sit down with Hana.
C. Put the trace up at Wednesday's leads meeting and ask Hana to walk everyone through it.
D. Drive out to the stand and show Hana the trace alone, before he talks to anyone else.

He finds her at dusk on the stand's upper deck, out of the wind behind the oxidizer tank, with her hood up and her hands in her sleeves. He gives her the printout. She holds it flat against the tank so it won't blow away. He asks what that August was like, and then he shuts up. She talks for a long time about the ground fault, three channels spiking for months, her and Wendell chasing it through every connector on two racks with flashlights in their teeth. I believed it was noise. I still mostly believe it. A gust takes the end of the sentence, and she waits for it to pass. Mostly is a terrible word for a valve. Below them a pronghorn crosses the access road, stops, and goes on. Sam asks if there's anything she wants him to know before he decides. If you open it, don't do it to me in a meeting. He tells her he won't. She looks at him then, for about a second, and hands the trace back folded smaller than he gave it to her.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Engaging a stakeholder starts with listening. Take the evidence to the person first, privately, and try to understand what they saw and why they decided what they did. Code 3.2.3 asks you to actively listen to other points of view, seeking to understand them, and 3.2.7 asks you, ideally, to go directly to the person you disagree with. The trust you build now is what lets the formal process work later.

Thursday, February 10. Sam had spent two days learning the anomaly process the way he'd once learned a new jet's tech orders, from the front. Anyone could open an anomaly report. Only a disposition could close one: explained and fixed, explained and accepted, or, when nobody could find a cause and the thing didn't happen again, UNR. Unexplained, not repeatable. Reopening a closed report took the program manager's signature and nothing else.

Nothing else on paper. Off paper, AR 2207 had been closed for seventeen months, and every test on the departure stage since had been built on the valve being fine. Quinn ran the numbers at lunch. A real investigation, if it came to a new test campaign, could cost the stand three to eight weeks, and the stand was already on the critical path.
At 4:30 Hana sent him one line. Whatever you decide, I'll run it straight.

The form was on his screen with the cursor blinking in the box that said REASON FOR REOPENING. It was 5:15, the light outside was going orange over the prairie, and the clock over the high bay doors said 738.
Hana says she'll run it straight, whatever he decides. What should Sam decide about AR 2207?
A. Leave AR 2207 closed and ask Hana to tell him if the valve ever acts up again.
B. Ask Aldergrove to recertify the valve in writing and attach the letter to the file.
C. Leave it closed for now and have Wendell take a quiet look at the old data first.
D. Reopen it at criticality 1 and give the investigation to Hana's team to run.

He types the reason in one sentence. Closure rationale not supported by independent evidence; failure mode is criticality 1 by consequence. He signs it. Then he calls Hana before the system can email her, so she hears it from him, and tells her the investigation is hers to run, with Wendell. Okay, she says. Then, after a while, Thank you for calling first. At 5:40 he sends the board's clerk a one paragraph notice. At 5:52 Garrett calls. Sam lets it ring, opens the trace, and calls him back at six and walks him through it. Garrett listens to the whole thing. That's three to eight weeks. Maybe. You know what you're doing to me. Yes. Garrett hangs up without saying goodbye, which with Garrett isn't the worst thing that can happen.

Exactly right. A closed report with a doubt behind it is an unmanaged risk with a signature on it. Reopening it puts it back where the process can see it, own it, and work it. Give it to the people who know the hardware, tell the person who made the original call before anyone else, and tell governance. Identify the risk honestly, then let the process do its job.
Decision four. One box with a door.

Monday, February 14. Valentine's Day, which Sam remembered at 6:50 AM because the grocery store in Bennett had a rack of red balloons by the door and he stood looking at it longer than a man buying coffee should. Grace had liked the cheap ones, the kind that went soft by Wednesday.

By eight he was in the program room for the argument the integrated plan had turned up. Bea's work breakdown structure covered the hardware down to the fasteners: three modules, the Breather, ground support, the launch campaign, a little over four hundred work packages. For flight software it had one box labeled SOFTWARE, and under it, in Bea's capitals, ASK RAFA.

Rafa had come ready. My scope is a backlog. Eleven hundred items, ranked. The top fifty are ready to build. The bottom four hundred are guesses with titles. If you make me turn that into work packages with dates, I'll do it, and it'll be fiction by the next demo.
Hana didn't look up from her laptop. And if the valve commands are a guess with a title, I requalify. Again.
Rafa's scope is a ranked backlog, and Hana needs valve commands that won't move. How should Sam structure the scope?
A. Add flight software to the WBS as one element whose content is Rafa's backlog.
B. Keep the WBS and the backlog as separate documents and compare them at each milestone.
C. Decompose the software backlog into dated work packages under the SOFTWARE element.
D. Move the hardware into Rafa's tool as epics and plan the whole ship sprint by sprint.

Quinn redraws the software box. Under it go the release milestones, tied to the hardware's red dates, and one line that points to Rafa's backlog as the element's content. Any backlog item that needs hardware has to name the WBS element it touches. Rafa reads it twice. So my whole team is one box. One box with a door in it. Does the door lock? On the red dates. Rafa thinks about it and says that's fair, which is the first time anyone in the room has heard him use the word.

That's a go. In a hybrid project the WBS can hold the whole scope while part of it stays adaptive. Decompose the hardware into work packages you can estimate and baseline. Put the software in as an element whose content is the ranked backlog, and tie its releases to the integration dates. One scope, two ways of managing it, and a seam somebody owns.

Wednesday, February 16. The scope statement was eleven pages, and the first ten were easy, because they said what the ship would do. Page eleven was the exclusions, and it was blank except for a sticky note Bea had left on the draft. DO THIS PART LAST. EVERYONE WILL HATE IT.
Quinn had pulled the items together from the 2058 requirements, the mass budget, and every meeting where somebody had asked for something and been told no. The biggest one was a single paragraph.

HALCYON PROJECT SCOPE STATEMENT DRAFT 3 SECTION 11, EXCLUSIONS. 11.1 Earth return. Halcyon carries no ascent vehicle and no return propellant. It will not bring any colonist, or its own crew, back to Earth. The crew of four remains at Ares Station until a return opportunity in a later window.. 11.2 Station expansion beyond the Breather, spare stacks, seed stock, and medical cargo.. 11.3 A second lander.. 11.4 Personal cargo above 2 kg per colonist.
Hale had read the draft over the weekend. Her note beside 11.1 was in blue ink: Do we have to say this? Garrett's, under hers: Call it "future capability." Investors like future.
Commander Yusra Haddad had four kids in Aurora. She'd read 11.1 too. She hadn't written anything.
Hale and Garrett both left notes beside section 11.1. What should Sam do with it?
A. Keep 11.1 plain and walk Hale and Commander Haddad through it before it's filed.
B. Leave the exclusions page out of this draft and settle 11.1 after the baseline.
C. Keep 11.1 as written and file the scope statement with the rest of the baseline.
D. Reword 11.1 as future capability, the way Garrett's note suggests, and keep the rest.

He takes Hale the mass budget and the reason in one sentence: the window gives them exactly enough lift for the Breather and the people to install it, and not one ascent vehicle more. If I sign that, I'm on record saying we're leaving four people on Mars. You're on record either way, ma'am. This way it's in your words. She signs it Friday. Haddad reads it in the gym at the training center in Aurora, still sweaty, feet up on a weight bench, and then reads it again. I signed up for one way in 2059. I'd like my husband to hear it from you before he reads it. On Saturday Sam sits at the Haddads' kitchen table for an hour. Four kids are being quiet on purpose in the next room, badly, and the youngest keeps coming in for water.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Define the scope, including what it won't do, and get agreement from the stakeholders it affects most. Plain words and a reason make the boundary something people can accept, or argue with honestly. Exclusions are where projects come apart later, so settle them on paper now.
Decision six. The last four hundred meters.

Friday, February 18, 2061. Two years to the day. Somebody on second shift had taped a paper party hat to the countdown clock over the doors, a gold one, a little crushed, and under it the clock said 730.

The Breather was the reason for the ship and the least broken down thing in it. Bea's WBS had one element for it, BREATHER (OXYGEN PLANT), with four boxes underneath: stacks, water, power, controls. The electrochemistry team was eleven people in a lab at the far end of the high bay where the air smelled like a swimming pool. Their lead, Owen Talbot, a soft spoken man with a beard he kept trimming shorter as the winter went on, had brought his own breakdown, and it was organized by who sat where.
These are my four groups, he said. That's the work.

Quinn drew his four boxes on the whiteboard. Under them she sketched the lander, and off to the right the station, and ran a line from one to the other. Then she stood there with the cap of the marker in her teeth and didn't say what the line was for.
Owen's breakdown has four boxes, one for each group. How should the Breather's work be broken down?
A. Keep Owen's breakdown by group, with stacks, water, power, and controls as the elements.
B. Use the Breather statement of work as the breakdown, one element per contract deliverable.
C. Break the Breather down by deliverable with Owen's team, down to work packages.
D. Break the Breather down to every task the team will do, tracked by the hour.

Two afternoons, most of the whiteboard, and a second box of markers. Plant hardware, yes, and also everything that has to exist before the plant can breathe for anybody: the install kit, the procedures, training for the station's engineers, a cutover from the old plant with no gap in it, the spares, and the test that proves the whole thing works at Mars pressure. When they add the pieces back up, Quinn finds what nobody owned. The last four hundred meters, from the lander to the plant room, across the regolith, at sixty below. I thought the station did that. The station thought we did. They write a WBS dictionary entry for every package, and Owen trims his beard again that weekend, which Quinn says is a good sign.

Exactly right. Decompose the scope by deliverable, with the people who'll do the work, down to work packages small enough to estimate and own. Then apply the 100 percent rule: the children have to add up to all of the parent and nothing outside it. That check is how you find the work that falls between teams.

Tuesday, February 22. Quinn had printed the risk register, because she said she couldn't think about it on a screen. Four hundred and twelve lines in eight point type, stapled at the corner, sorted by score the way it had always been sorted, highest first.
It took Sam twenty minutes to find the valve. It was on page nine.

HALCYON RISK REGISTER LINE 371 OF 412. R-0388 DEPARTURE STAGE MOIV-1 POSITION INDICATION ANOMALY (REF AR 2207). LIKELIHOOD 1 (RARE) IMPACT 3 (CRIT 2) SCORE 3. OWNER: PROPULSION RESPONSE: ACCEPT STATUS: CLOSED WITH AR
AR 2207 had been open again for twelve days. Its line in the register still said closed.
Directly above it, at line 370, was the risk that the program's coffee service contract would lapse. Score 4.

Sam read the top twenty. Most of them were written the way registers get written by tired people. Schedule pressure on stage integration. Thermal margin concerns. Nothing in any of them said what would happen to whom. He'd spent nine years on a flight line where the forms used plain words because the people reading them were nineteen and exhausted, and the plain words were part of what kept the nineteen year olds alive.
The valve is on page nine of the register. What should Sam do with that line?
A. Track the valve in the anomaly system only, and drop the duplicate line from the register.
B. Keep crit 2 but raise the likelihood to 3, moving the valve up into the top fifty.
C. Leave the valve line at crit 2 to match the closed report and the program's records.
D. Rewrite the valve line as crit 1 by its consequence, with likelihood marked unknown.

Quinn and Sam spend the afternoon rewriting the top forty lines in one form, his flight line form: if this happens, then this, and this is who gets hurt. The valve line becomes If the main oxidizer isolation valve fails to close on command at departure burn cutoff, the stage overburns, and the crew of four and the colony's air end up on a trajectory that doesn't reach Mars. Severity: crit 1. Likelihood: unknown, written as unknown. Owner: Hana. Trigger: any position disagreement, on any cycle, anywhere. Sorted by severity first, it's on page one. Wendell reads the new top forty standing at Quinn's desk and doesn't say anything for a while. Then he says, That's the first one of these I ever read all the way through.

That's a go. Identify and analyze risks honestly, and keep the two axes apart: impact comes from the consequence, likelihood from the evidence. If the likelihood is unknown, write unknown. Every risk needs an owner, a response, and a trigger, and the register has to be written so a tired person can read it and know what's at stake.

Thursday, February 24. Every requirement that touched the program lived in a compliance matrix, nine thousand rows, kept by an ARA mission assurance office in Denver that Sam had met exactly once. Quinn had spent two nights in it. After the register she'd wanted to know one thing: whether AR 2207 was the only report on Halcyon that had ever been downgraded.

It wasn't. There were four. All four had started at criticality 1 and been revised to criticality 2 with a rationale about test conditions, and each of them had closed in the month before a schedule review. Because each one was crit 2 on the day it closed, Flight Rule 2.36 showed against all four as not applicable.
AR 2207 was open again. The other three weren't. They were small things on the departure stage and the habitat: a heater, a pressure switch, a hatch latch.
None of them broke the rule, Quinn said. She had her hands flat on the table. That's what I can't stop looking at. Nobody broke it. They went around it the same way four times.
Quinn found four reports, all closed the same way. What should Sam do about it?
A. Restore crit 1 on all four and brief ARA mission assurance before telling the board.
B. Write up the pattern of four for the board and propose that it concur on downgrades.
C. Note in the matrix that all four closed at crit 2 and the rule was met each time.
D. Ask the ARA to grant a standing waiver of Flight Rule 2.36 for the departure stage.

Quinn pulls every downgrade back to 2058. There are four, and only these four. Sam sends the board a two page memo that names the reports, the dates, the reviews they came before, and what each rationale rested on. It names no people. At the bottom it proposes one control: no crit 1 report on Halcyon gets downgraded without the board's written concurrence. The clerk logs it as Question sixty one oh four for the March session. The next morning the clerk's acknowledgment comes back with the memo stamped and numbered, and in the margin, beside the stamp, a small tick in green ink. Docketed. R.C. Sam looks at the two letters for a while before he files it.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Confirm the compliance requirements, look for threats to them, and measure how far the project really complies. A workaround used four times is a threat to compliance even when every instance met the letter of the rule. Report it to the governance that owns the rule and propose a control that closes the gap. Code 2.3.1 asks you to uphold the rules that govern your work, and that includes what they're for.

Monday, February 28. 5:40 AM. One way light time this morning was six minutes and twenty eight seconds, the shortest it had been since Ada landed. In April it would bottom out a little over five, and Quinn had put a note on the program calendar that said CLOSEST, with no explanation, as if everyone would know what it meant. Everyone did.

A log from Ada Okafor, Ares Station. Sol 3565. One way, 6 minutes 28 seconds. Margin, 911 days. Hi, Dad. Sol 3565. I have tomatoes. Eleven of them, on the Bay C vines, red. Actually red. You don't know what red does to a person who's looked at orange dirt for two years. I'm cutting one into twelve pieces for the shift tonight, and Dr. Lindgren gets a piece, because she finally stopped asking about the basil. Your last log. I watched it twice, like always. You look tired in that kitchen light. It's the bulb over the table, Dad. It's been dying since I was in high school. Change the bulb. Okay. Real stuff. We had our first ration cut four sols ago. Hollis calls it a consumption adjustment. Calories down a tenth, three gym sessions a week instead of six, and the rec module goes dark at 2100 so we'll sleep more and breathe less. It's very scientific. It's also everybody hungry and in bed early, like a summer camp nobody signed up for. Hollis's report says it buys fifteen days. I ran it off the plant log, same as before. I get eight. So my number's nine hundred eleven by the time you hear this. I know what you're doing right now. You're doing subtraction on the back of something. One more thing, then tomatoes again. Teodor in the machine shop worked for a valve company in Pueblo before he came out. He says there's a woman there who's been arguing about one valve for twenty six years, and everybody at the company calls her the valve lady. He also says, and I'm only telling you what's going around the galley, that a valve on your ship did something weird in a test a couple of years ago and somebody closed the paperwork. Everybody here's heard it by now. Nobody here can check it. That's the bad part, up here. You hear a thing and there's nothing to do with it except hear it again at dinner. Have you met the valve lady? If she's real, I want to know what she's been arguing about. Remember the chore chart? Color coded, laminated, with a legend. I was nine. Mom said you'd made a Gantt chart for a fourth grader, and you said it was a responsibility matrix, and she laughed so hard she had to sit down on the stairs. I'm running the hydroponics expansion off a chart now. It's laminated. I hate that you were right. Love you. Nine hundred eleven. Ada out.

He got the gas bill out from under the fruit bowl. Under minus seventeen he wrote nine hundred eleven, and under that 920, the days from this morning to September 6, 2063. Minus nine. Eight days better on her number, because two hundred and twelve people were going to bed hungry at nine o'clock. Hollis's report, the one the ARA posted every Monday, would say 978, fifty eight to spare.
Then the valve. There was an old report. Eighteen days ago he'd reopened it. That was the true answer, and it was the only one he could give her yet, and it wasn't the whole of what she was asking.

At 9:20 Frances Odum called his cell. She didn't say hello. Malik's message came in this morning. He says they're on rations and in bed by nine, and Hollis calls it an adjustment. A breath. Families of Ares has a call Thursday. Two hundred people. Most of them have one question. They've heard the ship won't bring anybody home, and they want to know if it's true. Some of them have sick kids up there, Mr. Okafor. They want a seat.
Frances needs an answer for two hundred families on Thursday's call. How should Sam respond?
A. Tell Frances the program will look into a medical return option for the sickest colonists.
B. Write Frances a careful answer on what Halcyon won't carry, and why, for her call Thursday.
C. Join the families' call himself and tell them plainly that nobody comes home on Halcyon.
D. Ask ARA public affairs to take the families' call, with the program's facts in hand.

Thursday he sits in front of a laptop in the program room with two hundred faces on the screen and Frances in the corner tile. He says it the way it's written: nobody comes home on Halcyon. He says why, with the mass budget, in one sentence. Then he stops talking and asks what they need. It takes forty minutes. Most of them don't need a seat they know isn't there. They need the program's real forecast every month, with the odds. They need somebody at the program who answers email. They need to know which medicines are in the cargo. He writes it all down and commits to all three that week, with the email as his own job. At the end Frances says, That's the first time anybody from Tallgrass has told us something we didn't want to hear. She doesn't say thank you. She doesn't hang up first, either.

Exactly right. Managing expectations starts with finding out what they are. Then you align what the project will deliver with them, out loud, bad news included. Here the customers are the colonists and their families. Telling them what's excluded and asking what they need turns a fight over a seat into a list you can do something about.
Thursday, March 3. Hale came out to Watkins at noon with her chief of staff and a printout, and this time she sat down.

ARA OFFICE OF THE DIRECTOR REQUEST. Add an external camera to the habitat module to carry the departure burn and Mars arrival live. Countdown to Ares has offered to stream both free to its audience (40 million). Partners strongly in favor. Needed for the May partner meeting: confirmation that it's in the baseline.
Forty million people watching that ship leave, she said. Do you know what that does to a budget vote?

Rafa, who'd been asked to sit in, said the ship already had six navigation cameras, and he could probably stream two of them with a software change and no new hardware. Hana said probably was doing a lot of work in that sentence, since the navigation cameras fed guidance. Quinn wrote on her pad and turned it so Sam could read it. HAB MASS MARGIN 410 KG. EACH KG ON HAB COSTS ABOUT 2 KG OF PROPELLANT.

The change process written into the plan in February named a change board: Sam, the ARA's mission assurance lead, and Hale's deputy, with anything over a threshold going up to Hale. Hale was the sponsor. Today she was also the person asking.
Hale wants a camera on the habitat to stream the burn live. How should Sam handle it?
A. Add Rafa's streaming option to his team's backlog as a feature for the next sprint.
B. Log it as a change request and have the leads size both options for the change board.
C. Tell Hale no himself and point her to the habitat's 410 kilo mass margin.
D. Say yes to Hale at the table and have the habitat team work out the mounting details.

Sam tells Hale it'll be a change request by Friday and a decision in two weeks, with both options on it, and that she'll hear the answer before the partners do. She doesn't love the two weeks. The analysis turns up more than anybody expected. The hardware camera costs 31 kilos, about 62 of propellant, and a thermal rerun. Rafa's option costs no mass, but it needs a bus load test and a guidance requalification, which Hana insists on and Rafa, to his credit, agrees to. The change board approves Rafa's option, conditional on the test, and writes down why. Quinn sends Hale a one page status that afternoon. Hale reads it and says, You made me wait two weeks for a yes. For a yes you won't have to take back, ma'am.

That's a go. Every change, from anyone, takes the same path: write it down, analyze its impact on scope, schedule, cost, quality, and risk, decide it at the right level, update the plan, and tell the requester where it stands. A sponsor asking doesn't change the process. It makes doing the process well matter more.

Wednesday, March 9. 711 on the clock. Quinn's schedule was ready to baseline, which meant it was ready to become the thing every slip would be measured against for two years, which meant everybody wanted to change it today.

It had come up from the bottom: the leads' own estimates from January, the work packages from February, the Breather breakdown, Rafa's release milestones. AR 2207's investigation was in it too, Hana's estimate, three to eight weeks of stand time, sitting on the critical path like a rock in a creek. On the leads' own numbers, February 18 was still possible and still not likely.

Garrett had his own version. Someone in finance had moved the Breather's acceptance test two weeks earlier, into a week the stand looked free. Sam looked at the week. It was the week Wendell had blocked for the stand's seal change, which was written in Wendell's pocket notebook and nowhere else.
Baseline mine, Garrett said. It's got float on the 18th. Investors can read float.
Garrett wants his version baselined, with float on the 18th. What should Sam do about the baseline?
A. Baseline every software story with a date, along with the hardware work packages.
B. Baseline Quinn's bottom up version with software at the release level, through Hale.
C. Hold off on any baseline until the open technical questions close in the spring.
D. Baseline Garrett's version with the float on the 18th and sort out the stand later.

Quinn has the leads sign their sections one at a time at her cube, so nobody signs in a crowd. Rafa signs the release milestones and asks for the backlog itself to stay unbaselined, which is the whole point, and Quinn tells him so, and he looks pleased anyway. Hana signs, then asks to see the stand calendar one more time and reads it with her finger. Hale approves the baseline on the 11th with one line: Baselined on the team's estimates. Confidence reported monthly. Garrett wants the float explained to him in person. Halfway down the page he gets to the seal change and stops. Who knew about that? Wendell. Only Wendell? Until about ten this morning. Garrett takes his reading glasses off and taps them on the page twice, which is a thing Sam has never seen him do.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Prepare the schedule to fit the approach: hardware in detail, software at the level of releases tied to integration dates, the backlog left free to change. Build it from the estimates of the people doing the work, coordinate it with operations, then baseline it through governance. The baseline should measure the plan you actually have.
Decision twelve. On the lower number.

Monday, March 21. The Independent Readiness Board met in a federal building downtown, in a room with good chairs, bad coffee, and a seal on the wall nobody looked at. Seven members sat at a curved table. Ruth was at the end, with the green pen.
The program's integrated plan was due to the board by noon. It was finished. Sam had read every section of it, and he knew which parts he believed.
AR 2207 was in it, open, with Hana's investigation on the critical path.

What bothered him most wasn't the valve. Every date in the plan sat on one assumption, the ARA's oxygen margin model. On that model, arrival on September 6, 2063 left fifty eight days to spare. On the lower number Sam had seen, the one under his fruit bowl, the ship arrived nine days late. Nobody at the agency had yet said on the record which number was right.
Quinn had the cover memo open on her laptop. What do you want it to say?
The plan is due at noon, and every date rests on the agency's oxygen model. What's Sam's best move?
A. Send the plan with a one page note on its gaps, starting with the oxygen model.
B. Hold the plan back until the agency confirms its oxygen model, then submit it.
C. Send the summary that shows the plan supports February 18, and brief gaps if asked.
D. Send the board the full plan and all thirty one thousand schedule lines to judge.

The page has five lines. The first says the whole plan depends on the ARA's oxygen margin model, that station engineering data the program has seen runs about two months lower, and that on the lower number the plan arrives nine days late. The board reads it during the morning break. When the session resumes, Ruth asks the only question she asks all day. Mr. Okafor. On the lower number, does your plan get air there in time? No, ma'am. Not as it stands. The room goes quiet the way rooms do when somebody has said the thing. The chair asks the ARA's representative when the agency will verify its model. The representative says soon. The chair says May, and writes it down, and so does everybody else at the table.

Exactly right. Assess the consolidated plan for dependencies, gaps, and continued business value, and say what you found. The value here is air at Ares in time. If the plan can't show that on every credible number, the board needs to know in the first paragraph. Name the critical information the plan rests on, and ask for it to be verified.

Friday, March 25. Ruth's second page came in the mail, in a long envelope addressed in green ink with a Golden postmark and no return address. Sam didn't open it in the driveway. He set it on the kitchen table against the fruit bowl, made dinner, ate it standing at the counter, and kept an eye on the envelope the whole time, like a dog that might bolt.

AR 2207 had been open for six weeks. Hana's team had pulled every stand record from the summer of 2059, and Wendell had found the ground bus drawings in a flat file nobody had opened since the fault was fixed. Nothing they'd found yet said noise, and nothing said valve. Hana had started looking at him in meetings again. Not every time.
At eight he sat down with the tablet against the fruit bowl to answer the last thing in Ada's log. He'd answered the tomatoes weeks ago. He'd left the valve for last.

There's an old report on a valve. It's real. I reopened it. That's all I can tell you about it right now, and it's true, and when there's more I'll tell you more. He didn't do the voice. He watched it back once to make sure.
I haven't met the valve lady. If she's real, I'll find her. That part he meant all the way down.
It had been a good seven weeks, as these things went. He didn't trust the thought. It had the same shape as a thought he'd had once in Arizona, on a Thursday, with a pen in his hand.

He opened Ruth's envelope at 9:40. Page two was inside, the one about the timeline on the wall. Behind it was a photocopy folded into eighths and soft at the creases. He unfolded it on the table, pushing the fruit bowl back to make room.

It was the timeline. Eleven sheets shrunk onto one, so the bars were thin as thread. The red circles where the bars touched had gone gray in the copy. At the right edge, two vertical lines: the gate. Across the top, in Ruth's 2034 capitals, THE GATE IS REAL. THE BARS IN FRONT OF IT ARE GUESSES.
He found the propulsion row with his finger. Near the left, early in the flow, a short bar labeled ISOL VLV ACCEPT. In the margin beside it, in green ink, somebody had written a part number.
PETREL INTEGRATED TIMELINE MAY 2034 PROPULSION ROW (COPY). ISOL VLV ACCEPT. MARGIN, GREEN INK: 7740-112

He didn't need to check it. He checked it anyway. The printout of AR 2207 from that first night was in the drawer by the phone charger, under Grace's reading glasses, where he'd put it the night he brought it home from his desk in February, without exactly deciding to. He unfolded it next to the timeline. ALDERGROVE FLUID SYSTEMS PART NUMBER 7740-112, REV F.
Same supplier. Same number. Two valves, twenty five years apart.

The rest of the copy had faded the way photocopies of old pages fade, everything a little gray. The part number hadn't. It was the exact green of the pen in Ruth's cardigan pocket, and it sat on top of the gray the way new ink does.

He sat with the two pages side by side until the furnace came on and went off again. Then he got the gas bill out from under the fruit bowl, turned it over, and under minus nine he wrote 7740-112. He didn't know yet what it meant. He knew who did.
